title: Comparative phrases and clauses
subtitle: as normal a life as / too strong a word
summary: Build comparisons with as ... as, not as/such ... as, as many/much as, enough, too and so ... that / as to.

lesson.heading: as + adjective / adverb + as
lesson.text: We use **as ... as** to say that something or someone is like something or someone else, or that one situation is like another. The negative can use either **not as** or **not so**; in formal speech and writing **less** + adjective + **than** is more common.

examples.text: Was the film **as funny as** his last one?
I came round **as quickly as** I could.
The gap between the sides is **not as / so wide as** it was.
examples.note: or ... is less wide than it was.

lesson.heading: A noun inside the comparison
lesson.text: If we put a singular countable noun between the adjective and the second *as*, we need **a / an** in front of the noun. The negative can use **not as** + adjective + a/an + noun, or **not such a / an** + adjective + noun - but not a mixture of the two.

examples.text: Despite his disability, he tried to lead **as normal a life as** possible.
It's **not as quiet a place as** it used to be.
examples.note: or ... not such a quiet place as ...

examples.text: She's **not such a fluent Greek speaker as** she claims to be.

lesson.note: So, too and how work in the same way: It's not quite so straightforward a problem as it might at first seem. / 'Conspiracy' is perhaps too strong a word. / How big a piece do you want?

lesson.heading: as much / many as, as little / few as
lesson.text: These phrases say that a quantity or amount is larger or smaller than expected. **Many** and **few** are preferred before numbers; **much** and **little** are preferred with amounts (£40, 25%) and distances (50 metres).

examples.text: There are a small number of people involved, possibly **as few as** twenty.
Prices have increased by **as much as** 300%.
**As many as** 5,000 people phoned in to complain about last night's TV programme.

lesson.heading: not ... enough + to-infinitive
lesson.text: We use **not** + adjective / adverb + **enough** + to-infinitive to say that there isn't as much of something as is necessary. **Sufficiently** goes before the adjective or adverb and is often preferred in formal contexts.

examples.text: He **didn't speak loudly enough to** be heard.
She **didn't play sufficiently well to** qualify.

lesson.note: Choose one or the other: not ~~sufficiently well enough~~.

lesson.heading: too + adjective / adverb + to-infinitive
lesson.text: **Too** ... + to-infinitive means 'more than is necessary, possible or wanted' to do something. In rather formal English we can also use too + adjective + a / an + noun.

examples.text: They arrived **too late to** get seats.
It moved **too fast to** see it clearly.
The suitcase was **too small (for him) to** get all his clothes in.
I hope you haven't had **too tiring a day**.

lesson.heading: so ... that or so ... as to?

left.label: so + adjective / adverb + that-clause
left.text: The everyday pattern: something happened to such a degree that a particular result followed.
examples: It's **so simple that** even I can do it.
He came in **so quietly that** I didn't hear him.
The difference was **so small that** it wasn't worth arguing about.

right.label: so + adjective / adverb + as + to-infinitive
right.text: Less common, and more formal, but the same meaning.
examples: The difference was **so small as to** not be worth arguing about.
Her handwriting was **so untidy as to** be nearly illegible.

lesson.note: Use go so / as far as + to-infinitive for surprising or extreme actions: One furious woman went so / as far as to throw tomatoes at the minister.

lesson.text: With a singular noun inside the comparison the order is fixed: adjective + a/an + noun. *as normal a life as*, *too strong a word*, *how big a piece*.

exercises.prompt: I came round ___ as I could.
exercises.explanation: as + adverb + as compares how something was done.

exercises.prompt: ___ 5,000 people phoned in to complain about last night's TV programme.
exercises.explanation: Many is preferred before a number.

exercises.prompt: We don't use much electricity. Sometimes our bill is ___ £40 a month.
exercises.explanation: Little is preferred with amounts of money.

exercises.prompt: The Downtown Hotel is ___ to stay as the Strand Hotel.
exercises.explanation: Either not such a + adjective + noun, or not as + adjective + a + noun (not as pleasant a place as) - never a mixture.

exercises.prompt: The President's address to the nation is as ___ as he is ever likely to make in his career.
exercises.explanation: A singular countable noun inside the comparison needs a / an in front of it.

exercises.prompt: Which pair of words completes each sentence: as many/few as, or as much/little as?
categories: as many as / as few as
as much as / as little as

items.text: When it was really hot I was having ___ four showers a day.
The elephant population may soon fall to ___ 1,000 from 5,000 ten years ago.
At the end of the 200-metre race there was ___ 50 metres between the first and second runners.
Lit continuously, the life of a light bulb varies from ___ two weeks to three months.
Some days there were ___ three or four students at his lectures.
The country spends ___ 25% of its income on defence.

exercises.prompt: Join each first half to the clause that completes it with so + adjective + as + to-infinitive.

pairs.left: The noise from the factory was so loud

pairs.right: as to be almost impossible to move.

pairs.left: The CD was so badly scratched
The plot of the novel was so complicated
The difference between the results was so small

exercises.prompt: He didn't speak ___ to be heard at the back of the hall.
exercises.explanation: Enough follows the adjective or adverb: not + adverb + enough + to-infinitive.

exercises.statement: It's certainly enough bad to keep him out of football for at least six months.
exercises.explanation: It's certainly bad enough to keep him out of football ... Enough comes after the adjective, not before it.

exercises.prompt: Well, we all wish him ___ recovery as possible.
exercises.explanation: as + adjective + a + noun + as is the fixed order.

exercises.statement: I know him sufficiently well enough to say that he will consider his future carefully.
exercises.explanation: I know him sufficiently well / well enough to say ... Sufficiently and enough do the same job, so we use one or the other.

exercises.prompt: But I wouldn't go so far ___ say that he'll never play for the national team again.
exercises.explanation: go so / as far as + to-infinitive describes a surprising or extreme action.
